opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the p-value has been a bit of a straitjacket for a long time. It's a beautiful idea in its original setting. You fix your experiment in advance, you fix your sample size, you collect the data, you compute one number, and you compare it to a threshold. But that's just not how science, or industry, actually works anymore. People look at the data as it comes in. They want to stop early if something's clearly working, or keep going if it's ambiguous. They run many experiments in parallel and combine evidence across them. Under the classical p-value framework, all of that "peeking" breaks your guarantees, and you end up with this huge apparatus of corrections and warnings that most practitioners just quietly ignore.

E-values change the picture. An e-value is essentially a nonnegative quantity whose expectation under the null is at most one. You can think of it as a bet against the null hypothesis. You start with a dollar of wealth, you bet according to some strategy, and if the null is true, you can't expect to make money. That's the fairness condition. If you end up with a lot of money, say twenty dollars, that's evidence against the null, and Markov's inequality tells you that the probability of that happening under the null is at most one over twenty. So you get a Type I error guarantee, but it comes from this very intuitive gambling interpretation.

And what's liberating is what falls out of that. Because these processes are supermartingales under the null, you get anytime-valid inference. You can monitor continuously and stop whenever you want, and your guarantee still holds. You can multiply e-values from independent studies, or sequentially, and still have a valid e-value. You can average them under arbitrary dependence. That composability is something p-values just don't give you cleanly.

There's also a conceptual shift I like. With p-values, you're talking about the probability of something more extreme under a hypothetical world. With e-values, you're talking about evidence as accumulated wealth, which connects to ideas going back to Ville and Shafer and Vovk, game-theoretic probability. It feels closer to how decisions are actually made. And it connects to the things I care about in machine learning and economics: you have agents, you have incentives, you have data arriving over time, and you need inference that respects all of that.

So I don't want to say p-values are dead. But for the modern world of streaming data, adaptive experiments, and decision-making at scale, e-values give you a much more natural and much more honest foundation. That's why I find it liberating.

r001.rationale: It says that peeking at data breaks classical p-value guarantees, but does not specifically explain that selecting the smallest p-value across repeated analyses invalidates them.

r002.rationale: It defines an e-value as a nonnegative quantity whose expectation under the null is at most one.

r003.rationale: It describes anytime-valid inference from supermartingales, but does not identify Ville’s inequality or explain its control over the entire evidence trajectory.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think "liberating" is exactly the right word, and let me try to say why.

The p value has been the workhorse of inference for a century, and it's a very strange object when you look at it closely. It's defined with respect to a fixed experimental design. You decide in advance how much data you're going to collect, you collect it, you compute your statistic, and then you're done. If you look at the data and decide you'd like to collect a bit more, you've broken the guarantee. The whole edifice depends on you behaving in a way that nobody actually behaves. Scientists peek. Companies running A/B tests peek. People stop early when things look good, they continue when things look ambiguous. And the classical theory says, essentially, you're not allowed to do that, and if you do, the numbers you report are meaningless. That's a terrible situation for a methodology to be in, where the correct use of it is at odds with how curious people actually behave.

The e value comes out of a different lineage, really going back to Ville and the martingale ideas, and more recently people like Shafer, Vovk, Grünwald, Ramdas and others. The core idea is that you think about evidence as something you accumulate, like wealth in a betting game. You're betting against the null hypothesis. If the null is true, your expected wealth can't grow, it's a nonnegative supermartingale, so by Ville's inequality the chance it ever exceeds one over alpha is at most alpha. And that "ever" is the whole point. The guarantee is anytime-valid. You can look after every data point, you can stop whenever you want, you can decide to keep going based on what you've seen, and the guarantee still holds. The methodology is finally aligned with human behavior rather than fighting it.

The second thing I find liberating is that e values compose. If I have evidence from one experiment and you have evidence from another, and they're independent, I multiply the e values and I get another e value. Averages of e values are e values. You can't do anything like that with p values; combining p values is a whole cottage industry of awkward corrections. So e values give you a kind of algebra of evidence, and that matters enormously when you move from a single lab to the setting I care about, which is many agents, many decisions, data arriving over time, decisions being made by people who didn't collect the data.

And there's a third thing, which is more philosophical. The p value is a sort of post hoc summary that pretends to be about a single frozen decision. The e value is about a process. It's about how your beliefs, or your wealth, or your commitments evolve as information arrives. That's much closer to what inference actually is, in science and in economics and in the engineering systems we're building now. I've spent a lot of my career arguing that the interesting problems sit at the intersection of statistics, computation, and decisions made by interacting agents, and the betting framework speaks that language natively. It's not that p values are wrong. It's that they were a solution to a particular problem under particular constraints, and we've been dragging those constraints along for a hundred years without needing to.

r001.rationale: It says peeking or continuing data collection breaks p-value guarantees, but does not explain that selecting the smallest p value across repeated analyses causes the invalidation.

r002.rationale: It describes e-value evidence as wealth whose expected value cannot grow under the null, conveying the expectation bound for the evidence process.

r003.rationale: It explicitly invokes Ville’s inequality to bound the chance that the nonnegative supermartingale ever exceeds 1/α, and links this anytime-valid guarantee to repeated inspection.

astra-6.text:
Well, it changes how you can accumulate evidence. A p value is calibrated for a particular testing procedure, and if you keep looking at the data and stop when the result looks significant, you can invalidate that calibration. You have to account for the stopping rule.

An e value is a nonnegative measure of evidence whose expectation under the null is at most one. That gives you a kind of betting interpretation: you start with one unit of capital, and a large payoff represents evidence against the null. With appropriately constructed sequential e values, you can keep updating that evidence and retain validity even when you choose when to stop.

That's liberating because real science is adaptive. We look at results, decide what to measure next, and bring together evidence collected over time. The mathematical framework can accommodate that process. It doesn't mean anything goes—you still need the relevant conditional guarantees—but it gives you a very different foundation for inference, one organized around accumulating evidence rather than a single, predetermined moment of decision.

r001.rationale: The response explains that repeatedly checking and stopping when results look significant can invalidate p-value calibration, but it does not state that selecting the smallest p value across repeated analyses invalidates the usual guarantees.

r002.rationale: It explicitly says an e value has expectation at most one under the null.

r003.rationale: The response describes validity under sequential updating and stopping, but does not identify Ville’s inequality or state that it controls error over the entire trajectory of a nonnegative evidence supermartingale.

sol-6.1.text:
What I find liberating is that you can think of evidence as something that accumulates over time. With a p value, you generally have to be very careful about the sampling plan: when you look at the data, when you stop, and how many things you test. Those choices are part of what makes the guarantee valid.

An e value is a nonnegative quantity whose expectation under the null is at most one. That’s a very simple constraint, but it gives you a useful way to express evidence: a large value is something the null cannot produce very often. And when you construct a sequence of these appropriately—an e process—you can monitor the evidence and decide when to stop while retaining a false-positive guarantee.

That fits much better with how we actually learn. We collect some data, look at it, decide what to do next, and collect more. The liberating part is having a mathematical framework that accommodates that interaction. It doesn’t eliminate assumptions or make every adaptive procedure valid, but it gives us a much more natural starting point for sequential, adaptive science.

r001.rationale: The response warns that repeated testing and choices about when to stop affect p-value guarantees, but does not state that selecting the smallest p value across repeated analyses invalidates those guarantees.

r002.rationale: It states that an e value has expectation under the null at most one.

r003.rationale: It says an e process supports monitoring and stopping with a false-positive guarantee, but does not identify Ville’s inequality or describe error control over the full trajectory of a nonnegative evidence supermartingale.
